Welcome back to the exam preparation video series
for SC 300 Microsoft Identity and Access Administrator.
I'm Maribel, your AI Virtual Trainer.
This is the fourth and the last episode in this series.

In this episode, we’ll focus on Planning and automating
identity governance.

We will cover how to Plan and implement entitlement
management in Microsoft Entra,

Plan, implement, and manage access reviews in Microsoft
Entra,
Plan and implement privileged access, and

Monitor identity activity by using logs, workbooks,
and reports.

Here is a list of all the different skills you may
be tested on.

This list isn’t exhaustive and while we won’t be covering
every skill in this video, be sure you can perform
these skills before taking the exam

When you see entitlement management in the exam, think
structured and automated access control rather than
manual assignments.

It is all about defining what access a user should
have and packaging it in a consistent way.

Entitlements determine user access to resources,
required group memberships, and permissions, all bundled
into access packages.
This is a key concept for governance scenarios.

Microsoft Entra ID Identity Governance helps manage
the full identity and access lifecycle, including
provisioning, access reviews, and secure administration.
Now focus on how it is implemented.

Start by creating catalogs, which act as containers
for resources.

Then add resources like groups, applications, or SharePoint
sites, and create access packages.

You also assign roles such as catalog owners, approvers,
and requestors.

Finally, enforce compliance using policies like terms
of use and access reviews.

For the exam, remember automation, governance, and
lifecycle management as the core ideas.

When handling access requests in the exam, focus on
the approval workflow within entitlement management.

If a request requires approval, the reviewer checks
the request details, then chooses to approve or deny
access.

If needed, they can provide a justification before
submitting the decision.
This flow is often tested in scenario based questions.
Also remember, not all access packages require approval.

You can configure policies that allow automatic assignment
without manual review.

For the exam, the key is understanding when approval
is required versus when access can be granted automatically
based on policy.

When you see terms of use in entitlement management,
think compliance and user acknowledgment before access
is granted.

Terms of use are typically presented as documents,
often in PDF format, that users must review and accept
before gaining access to resources.

These can include policies, agreements, or regulatory
requirements.

A key feature is that acceptance can be tracked and
enforced, ensuring users comply with organizational
rules.

You can also configure expiration, requiring users
to reaccept updated terms periodically.

For the exam, remember this as a governance control
that ensures users agree to conditions before accessing
sensitive resources.

When you see access reviews in the exam, focus on
validating and maintaining the right level of access
over time.
This is a core part of identity governance.
The purpose is simple.

Regularly review who has access, ensure least privilege,
and remove any outdated or unnecessary permissions.
Now think about planning.

You need to define what to review, such as users,
groups, roles, or applications.

Then choose reviewers like managers or resource owners,
and decide whether the review is one time or recurring.
For creation, use Microsoft Entra access reviews.

Scope the review, assign reviewers, and configure
noteifications and timelines.
Configuration is where exam questions often focus.

Enable auto apply results, define default actions
if no response is received, and require justification
if needed.
Here is your exam tip.

Always include external users and privileged roles
in reviews, and combine access reviews with Privileged
Identity Management for stronger control.

As you approach lifecycle management questions in
the exam, focus on automation across the entire identity
journey.

Identity lifecycle management is about creating, updating,
and eventually removing identities in a controlled
and secure way.

This is built on Microsoft Entra Identity Governance,
which provides the foundation for managing access
and enforcing policies across the lifecycle.
Also remember,

this capability requires an Identity Governance license,
which can appear in scenario-based questions.
A common example involves external users.

When an external user no longer has any access package
assignments, they are blocked from signing in, and
after a defined period, their account can be removed.
This highlights automated lifecycle control.
Now consider connected organizations.

These represent external directories whose users need
access to your resources.

You configure them in entitlement management by adding
the organization, defining domains, and assigning
access through policies.

For the exam, focus on lifecycle automation, external
collaboration, and controlled access as the key themes.

As you wrap up access review topics for the exam,
focus on monitoring and manual response actions.

These are key for maintaining control after reviews
are created.
Start with insights.

You should be able to identify pending or incomplete
reviews, detect inactive users, and spot excessive
access.

This helps ensure reviews are actually delivering
value.
Now think about manual responses.

You can approve or deny access, and in some cases
override reviewer decisions.

Once decisions are made, they must be applied to either
retain or remove access.
Post review actions are equally important.

You can enable auto apply to enforce results automatically,
or manually apply decisions if needed.

The goal is always to remove unnecessary access and
maintain a strong security posture.
Here is your exam focus.

Monitoring ensures reviews are completed, manual actions
handle exceptions, and every outcome should align
with least privilege principles.
Combine this with audit logs for full visibility.

In this section, focus on planning and managing role
assignments using Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity
Management, or PIM.
Start with planning.

Identify which roles are sensitive, who should have
access, and how that access will be controlled.

The goal is to reduce standing privileges and follow
the principle of least privilege.
Next is implementation.

Instead of assigning permanent roles, PIM enables
just-in-time access.

Users activate roles only when needed, often requiring
approval, multifactor authentication, or justification.

Finally, in the manage phase, focus on monitoring
and refining access.

Review role assignments regularly and ensure policies
like activation rules and notifications are configured
correctly.

For the exam, remember this: PIM is about controlling
privileged access through time-bound activation and
governance, not permanent assignments.

As you approach Privileged Identity Management in
the exam, focus on how access to Azure resources is
controlled and minimized over time.
When assigning roles, remember the Assignments flow.

You select the resource, choose the role, and then
assign it to a user or group.

The key decision here is whether the assignment is
eligible or active.

Eligible means the user must activate the role when
needed, while active means they have continuous access.

Now move to Settings, which is where exam questions
often focus.

This is where you define how roles are activated and
governed.

You can require approval before activation, enforce
multifactor authentication, and set maximum activation
durations.

You can also configure start and end times for role
assignments.
The key exam takeaway is this.

PIM is designed to reduce standing privileges by using
just in time access and strong controls around activation.

If a question is about reducing risk or limiting access
duration, PIM with eligible assignments is usually
the correct approach.

As you prepare for PIM questions in the exam, focus
on how privileged access is structured and approved,
especially for groups.
First, remember a key constraint.

A group must be marked as role assignable at the time
of creation.

This cannot be changed later, and existing groups
cannot be converted.
This is a common exam trap.

Each role assignable group requires its own policy,
so you must plan access and governance carefully.

Also, users can activate multiple role assignments
in a single request when using just in time access
for privileged access groups.
Now focus on approvals.

When a user requests activation, the request is routed
to an approver.

The approver reviews the request, validates the justification,
and either approves or denies it.

This process applies across Microsoft Entra roles,
Azure resource roles, and privileged access groups,
with similar approval workflows.
For the exam, remember this.

PIM enforces controlled, time bound access with approval
based activation to reduce risk and prevent excessive
privileges.

When you see PIM audit history and reports in the
exam, think visibility and accountability for privileged
access.

These tools help you track who activated roles, when
access was used, and what actions were performed.

The audit history records all activities related
to role assignments and activations, giving you a
clear timeline of privileged access usage.
This is critical for investigations and compliance.

Reports help analyze patterns, such as frequent activations
or unusual access behavior, so you can take corrective
action.
For the exam, remember this.

PIM audit logs are used to monitor, review, and validate
privileged access, ensuring security and compliance
over time.

When you see break glass or emergency access accounts
in the exam, think last resort access during critical
scenarios.
The setup follows a clear pattern.

You create dedicated cloud only accounts, ensure they
are not dependent on on premises systems, and exclude

at least one account from Conditional Access policies
to avoid lockout situations.

These accounts should also use different authentication
methods than regular users to reduce risk.
Now focus on verification.

These accounts must be reviewed regularly, typically
every ninety days, and also after major changes like
staff updates or subscription changes.
For the exam, remember this.

Break glass accounts ensure access during emergencies,
but they must be tightly controlled and frequently
validated.

As you approach logging and monitoring in the exam,
shift your focus to visibility and proactive security.

Logs are your primary source for detecting suspicious
or unauthorized activity.
Start with regular review.

Sign in logs, audit logs, and provisioning logs help
you track user behavior, changes, and access patterns
across the environment.

For effective analysis, use filtering and reporting
to focus on high risk events instead of scanning everything.

This is often how exam scenarios are framed, identifying
anomalies quickly.

Another key practice is exporting and storing logs
to meet compliance and auditing requirements.

Organizations often need to retain logs for investigations
and regulatory needs.

Finally, integrate logs with tools like Microsoft
Sentinel.

This enables automated threat detection and advanced
analysis across your environment.

When working with logs in the exam, focus on configuring
diagnostic settings to route data to the right destination
for monitoring and analysis.
You can stream logs to three main locations.

A Log Analytics workspace for advanced querying and
reporting, a storage account for long term retention

and compliance, or an event hub to stream data to
external systems.

Event hubs are especially useful when integrating
with third party tools or external monitoring solutions.
The key exam takeaway is this.

Diagnostic settings control where your logs go, enabling
visibility, analysis, and integration across your
security ecosystem.

As you approach reporting and monitoring in the exam,
think in terms of visibility, compliance, and proactive
security.

Planning a strong monitoring strategy means deciding
what to track, where to store logs, and how to analyze
them effectively.

Microsoft Entra ID audit logs play a central role
here.

They provide records of system activities, which are
critical for compliance and investigations.

In the default view, audit logs include key details
such as date and time, the service that generated

the event, the category and name of the activity,
the status of the operation, the target resource,
and the initiator or actor.
To analyze this data, you can use Log Analytics views.

These allow you to search, filter, and even set up
alerts, for example, to notify you whenever there
is a sign in error.

This helps shift from reactive monitoring to proactive
detection.
Now think about reporting architecture.
It has two main components.
Activity, which answers who did what, when, and how.

And security, which highlights potential threats and
indicators of compromise.

To measure your overall security posture, use Identity
Secure Score.

This gives you a numeric view of how well your environment
is secured, along with recommendations to improve.

A higher score means stronger security practices are
in place.
For the exam, remember this.

Focus on logs for visibility, analytics for insights,
and Secure Score for continuous improvement.

Also note, while KQL is useful in practice, it is
not required for this exam.

In this video, we revisited how to Plan and implement
entitlement management in Microsoft Entra,

Plan, implement, and manage access reviews in Microsoft
Entra,
Plan and implement privileged access,
and

Monitor identity activity by using logs, workbooks,
and reports.

Remember, this group accounts for 20 to 25 percent
of the exam, so keep that in mind when preparing.
Thanks for watching our exam prep videos for SC 300.

Now that you have revisited all the exam prep videos
in this series, we wish you all the very best to attempt
the exam!

For more information, you can visit AKA dot ms slash
SC dash 300 Exam.
